newsitem.title: CANADA: Worldwatch's Brown sees Asia grain demand as key.
newsitem.headline: Worldwatch's Brown sees Asia grain demand as key.

text.p: Population growth and problems with water management in Asia should drive up demand for grains steadily in coming decades, Worldwatch Institute's director Lester Brown said on Thursday.
"The rate of population growth in some central Asian states is higher than in India, so there will be an increasing need to import grain," Brown said in a speech to the Winnipeg Chamber of Commerce.
Brown, whose 1995 book "Who Will Feed China?" predicted China may import 200 million tonnes of grain a year by 2030, said aquifers in north China and India's Punjab were dropping.

"Northern India's facing the same problem as China. The Punjab, the breadbasket of India, is experiencing a steady depletion of its underground water and it will be faced with some substantial irrigation cutbacks," Brown said.
Another source of demand for water comes from urbanization where expanding cities such as Beijing and Los Angeles compete with surrounding rural areas for water use, he said.
"In a country like China, the loss of irrigation water translates into the need for additional grain imports," Brown said. "To import a tonne of wheat is to, in effect, import 1,000 tonnes of water."
Southern China has also been losing rice crop land to urban sprawl with increases in yields unable to make up the loss, Brown said.
"China can import a lot of grain but who can supply them? No one can on that scale," Brown said.

Kazakhstan, a traditional supplier of grain to Russia, may need to import grain in coming years as would other central Asian republics such as Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan and Uzbekistan due to rapid increases in population growth, he said.

To meet such demand, production will have to continue rising in major exporters. Argentina could double its grain exports to 24 million tonnes from 12 million in coming years and Ukraine may also expand grain output, Brown said.
